chapters.title: Chapter 4: Calls, Covered Calls, and Collars

lessons.title: The Collar: Using Call Premium to Pay for a Put

children.text: By now you have met two tools that pull in opposite directions. A protective put costs money and protects the downside. A covered call earns money and caps the upside. Put them together on the same holding and the premium from one pays for the other. That combination is a collar, and it is how many investors approaching a goal lock in a range of outcomes for close to zero upfront cost. The catch is right there in the name. A collar holds you in from both sides. You cannot fall through the floor, and you cannot rise through the ceiling.

body.text: A collar trades away gains above a ceiling to pay for protection below a floor. A zero-cost collar is not free protection. It is protection paid for with upside you may never get to keep.

children.text: The Three Legs of a Collar

markDefs.definition: Owning an asset, buying an out-of-the-money put below the current price and selling an out-of-the-money call above it, so returns are confined between a floor and a cap.
A collar where the premium received from the call roughly equals the premium paid for the put, so the net upfront cost is close to zero.

children.text: A
collar

has three parts: the holding you own, a put you buy below today's price, and a call you sell above it. The put sets the floor. The call sets the cap. The difference between the two premiums is your net cost, which can be a small debit, a small credit, or close to nothing. When it is close to nothing, the structure is called a
zero-cost collar

body.latex: \begin{aligned} \text{Net cost per unit} &= P_{put} - C_{call} \\ \text{Maximum loss per unit} &= (S_0 - K_{put}) + \text{Net cost} \\ \text{Maximum gain per unit} &= (K_{call} - S_0) - \text{Net cost} \end{aligned}
body.caption: S₀ = price today, K = strikes, P and C = premiums. A negative net cost is a net credit, which reduces the maximum loss and increases the maximum gain.

children.text: Worked Example: Collaring a Nifty Index Fund

Anand, 57, is a senior manager at a steel company in Jamshedpur. He holds ₹32,50,000 in a Nifty 50 index fund, which is 130 Nifty units or two lots at 25,000. He retires in three months and wants protection for that window, but the ₹32,500 cost of two lots of the 24,000 put feels steep. So he looks at selling two lots of a three-month call to pay for it.

body.caption: Three-month Nifty collars on 130 units, Nifty at 25,000, all using the 24,000 put at ₹250 (illustrative model premiums)

children.text: The pattern is the familiar one: the closer the call, the more it pays, and the lower the cap. Anand picks the 24,000 / 26,500 collar. For just ₹2,600 upfront, his portfolio's result over three months is confined to a range between losing 4.1% and gaining 5.9%.

stats.label: Net upfront cost
stats.context: ₹32,500 paid for puts, ₹29,900 received for calls

body.caption: Anand's ₹32,50,000 portfolio at expiry: unhedged, put only, and 24,000 / 26,500 collar (illustrative)

body.title: Unhedged vs protective put vs collar at expiry

children.text: Between 24,000 and 26,500, the collar beats the put-only hedge by ₹29,900 in every scenario, because the call premium has paid for the protection. Above 26,500, the lines cross. At 28,000 the put-only investor is up ₹3,57,500 while Anand is stuck at ₹1,92,400. That ₹1,65,100 gap is the real price of his "zero-cost" protection, paid only if the market rallies hard.

body.text: A three-month move from 25,000 to 28,000 is 12%. That sounds large, but strong quarters do happen. Calendar year 2023, for example, saw the Nifty rise about 20%. A collar suits Anand precisely because he has a near-term goal and values certainty over the chance of a big rally. For a 35-year-old with a 20-year horizon, giving up the best quarters of a bull market would be a very expensive trade.

body.title: What does zero-cost really mean?
body.question: An investor sets up a collar where the call premium exactly matches the put premium. Which statement is true?
options: The protection is completely free in every scenario
There is no upfront cost, but gains above the call strike are given up
The investor can no longer lose money on the holding
The investor earns the call premium on top of any rally
body.explanation: Zero-cost refers only to the upfront cash. The investor pays for the put by agreeing to give up all gains above the call strike. They can still lose money down to the put strike, and they do not keep gains above the call strike.

body.title: Name the legs
body.textWithBlank: A collar combines the holding, a long out-of-the-money put and a short out-of-the-money ___.
body.explanation: The long put creates the floor, and the short call creates the cap. The call premium offsets some or all of the put premium.

children.text: Collars on Stocks vs Collars on Index Funds

A collar on shares you own is the cleanest version. If the stock ends above the call strike, the shares are delivered at that strike and the call's obligation is met. If it ends below the put strike, you deliver the shares at the put strike instead. Either way, the shares themselves settle the options.

body.title: A stock collar's worst case
body.prompt: Suresh owns 400 shares at ₹1,500, one lot in this example. He buys the 1,400 put at ₹12 and sells the 1,650 call at ₹10. What is his maximum total loss at expiry, in rupees?
body.explanation: Net cost = ₹12 − ₹10 = ₹2 per share. Maximum loss per share = (1,500 − 1,400) + 2 = ₹102. Total = 102 × 400 = ₹40,800. His maximum gain is (1,650 − 1,500) − 2 = ₹148 per share, or ₹59,200.

children.text: A collar on a mutual fund portfolio, using Nifty options, is economically similar but practically very different. The fund cannot be delivered against the options, so every leg settles in cash on its own.

body.title: Stock collar vs index fund collar

columns.label: Collar on shares you own
points: Options are physically settled against your shares
A strong rally ends with shares sold at the call strike, no extra cash needed
Short call margin can often be supported by pledging the shares
Selling the shares at the cap triggers capital gains tax
Needs a stock with liquid options and at least one full lot

columns.label: Collar on an index fund using Nifty options
points: Options settle in cash, the fund stays untouched
A strong rally means paying the call's loss in cash while the fund's gain stays on paper
The short call needs full margin, which can be ₹2 lakh or more per lot
Basis risk applies if the funds do not track the Nifty closely
Taxes on the options and the fund are calculated separately

body.text: The cash-settlement problem is serious. If the Nifty rallies to 28,000, Anand's two short 26,500 calls lose (28,000 − 26,500) × 130 = ₹1,95,000, which must be paid in cash. His fund has gained ₹3,90,000, but only on paper. He needs that ₹1,95,000 available in his trading account, or he must redeem fund units, possibly with tax, to meet it. Margin requirements also rise as the market moves towards the call strike, so he may need extra cash well before expiry.

body.title: The collar in a runaway rally
body.scenario: Anand sets up his 24,000 / 26,500 collar on two lots with the Nifty at 25,000 and just ₹60,000 of spare cash in his trading account beyond the margin blocked on day one. Six weeks later, strong foreign inflows push the Nifty to 26,800. His broker messages him about additional margin on the short calls. Anand is annoyed: "My fund is up ₹2.34 lakh, why am I being asked for money?"
body.prompt: Explain what is happening to Anand's position and what his realistic choices are.
body.modelAnswer:
1. His fund is up (26,800 − 25,000) × 130 = ₹2,34,000, but that gain sits in mutual fund units, not in his trading account.
2. His short 26,500 calls are now in the money with six weeks left, so they have lost significant value, and the exchange requires more margin as they move against him. The long 24,000 puts are now almost worthless.
3. Choice one: add cash and hold. If the Nifty stays above 26,500 at expiry, he pays the call loss in cash, and his total gain is capped at about ₹1.92 lakh, as designed.
4. Choice two: buy back the calls now, at a loss, to remove the cap and the margin problem. He keeps the rally from here, but the protection he got was paid for with that loss.
5. Choice three: roll the calls up to a higher strike. This means buying back the 26,500 calls and selling, say, 27,500 calls, which usually costs a net debit but raises the cap.
6. Choice four: redeem some fund units to raise cash, accepting any tax and exit load.
The lesson: a collar on an index fund needs a cash buffer sized for the worst-case call loss, not just the day-one margin. This is the practical cost that a zero-cost label hides.

body.title: Adjusting a collar when the market heads for the cap

children.text: Collars are not set-and-forget. If the underlying rallies towards the call strike well before expiry, you have three standard moves:
Do nothing:
accept the cap. This is the right answer if the collar was designed around a goal and the capped gain is enough.
Roll the call up:
buy back the current call and sell a higher strike. This raises the cap, usually for a net debit.
Roll the whole collar up:
close both options and open a new put and call around the higher market level. This locks in part of the rally with a higher floor, at the cost of a new round of premiums and transaction charges.
The Advanced Options Strategies for Portfolio Protection course covers rolling and strike management in depth.

body.title: Before you set up a collar
steps: Confirm that giving up gains above a cap fits your goal. Collars suit near-term goals, not long-horizon compounding.
Choose the put strike from your tolerable drawdown first, then find the call strike that brings net cost to a level you accept.
Write down the floor, cap, maximum loss and maximum gain in rupees for the full period.
For index fund collars, calculate the cash you would need if the Nifty ended 10% above the call strike, and keep that buffer available.
Check your broker's margin for the short call, and decide in advance whether you would hold, roll or close if the market nears the cap.

body.label: NSE Option Chain
body.description: Compare put premiums below and call premiums above the current Nifty level for the same expiry to find a collar with the net cost you want.

cards.definition: Holding + long OTM put + short OTM call. Returns are confined between a floor and a cap.
A collar where the call premium roughly equals the put premium, so there is little or no upfront cost.
The put strike. Below it, the put offsets further losses.
The call strike. Above it, the short call gives up further gains.
Put premium − call premium. A negative figure is a net credit.
Buying back a short call and selling a higher strike to raise the cap, usually for a net debit.

points: A collar combines a long put for a floor with a short call for a cap, using the call premium to pay for the put.
Maximum loss = (S₀ − put strike) + net cost. Maximum gain = (call strike − S₀) − net cost.
A zero-cost collar costs nothing upfront, but the real price is every rupee of gain above the cap.
Collars suit investors with near-term goals who value certainty over the chance of a big rally.
Stock collars settle against your shares. Index fund collars settle in cash and need a cash buffer for call losses in a rally.
Short calls need margin that rises as the market approaches the cap. Plan for it before you start.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Option premiums, margin estimates and investor examples are illustrative. Actual margin requirements depend on your broker and exchange rules at the time. Selling options carries risk. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before using collars.
